objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer:
This is a fair pressure point, and you're right that *prōtotokos* naturally carries birth-order connotations in many contexts — but Paul's own sentence structure settles the question before ambiguity can even take root. He calls Christ "firstborn over all creation" and then, in the very next clause, grounds that title with "for by Him were all things created" (Colossians 1:16). If Paul meant Christ was the first item within creation, he has just made his own argument incoherent: the "firstborn" would be creating the category He belongs to, including Himself. That's not a plausible reading of a careful theological argument; it's a self-contradiction Paul had every reason to avoid and no reason to invite.

The "rank and inheritance" sense of *prōtotokos* isn't a later retrofit — it's attested within Scripture's own usage. Psalm 89:27 has God call David "my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth," despite David being neither God's literal offspring nor even the eldest son of Jesse. So the semantic range Paul draws on already existed in the Jewish scriptures he was steeped in; he's not coining a novel meaning to dodge Arius three centuries early.

And the immediate context of Colossians 1 reinforces this rank-reading rather than fighting it: Christ is "the image of the invisible God," all things visible and invisible were created through Him and for Him, and He is "before all things" and the one "in [whom] all things hold together." That is Creator-language, not creature-language. Paul isn't retrofitting homoousios onto a stray word; he's using an inheritance-title precisely because Christ's supremacy over creation, not His place within it, is his entire point in that passage.

So the choice isn't between "Paul picked a misleading word" and "the doctrine came later." It's that Paul used a title whose biblical precedent (Psalm 89) already meant preeminent heir, and he immediately clarified it in case anyone missed it — which is exactly what you'd expect from someone defending, not obscuring, the Son's full deity.

Paul writes in Colossians 1:15 that Christ is the *prōtotokos* of creation — and in Greek, *prōtotokos* has a straightforward meaning tied to birth-order and temporal priority. If he meant "preeminence" or "sovereignty," why not say that directly, the way he does elsewhere? The word's first-century usage — whether in LXX translations, in pagan texts, or in Jewish sources — consistently points to *firstborn* as literally the first offspring. Arians seized on this for good reason: it's the most natural reading. So either Paul is saying Christ was the first created being, or he's using a term that unavoidably sounds like he is — and then later theology has to retrofit a non-literal meaning onto it to defend homoousios.
